B1:
Cause: Touched fires once for every body part that touches the brick (feet, legs and so on), and it can fire several times per part before anything takes effect. Each event adds 10. Destroy() doesn't stop events that are already queued, especially with deferred signals. So you get 30-50 coins.

Fix: add a debounce flag that is set before granting, and make the grant happen only once.
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local collected = false
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if collected then return end
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if not plr then return end
    local hum = hit.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    collected = true
    plr.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 10
    part:Destroy()
end)
```
For respawning coins, use a per-player cooldown table (cleared on PlayerRemoving) instead of destroying the part. Run this on the server.
B2:
Diagnosis: with StreamingEnabled, the client only has instances near the player. Far-away parts of the map, like distant doors, aren't streamed in when the LocalScript runs, and they can stream out again later. Dot-indexing a missing child throws "Door is not a valid member of Model". The doors near spawn work because they are already loaded.

Fix 1: tag-driven (preferred). Tag the doors "Door" with CollectionService and handle them as they stream in and out.
```lua
local CS = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local function setup(door)
    door.Touched:Connect(onTouch)
end
for _, d in CS:GetTagged("Door") do setup(d) end
CS:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door"):Connect(setup)
```
Connections on doors that stream out are cleaned up when those instances are removed.

Fix 2: wait for the instance with a timeout.
```lua
local hotel = workspace.Map.Buildings:WaitForChild("Hotel", 10)
local door = hotel and hotel:WaitForChild("Door", 10)
```
Set the Hotel model's ModelStreamingMode to Atomic, so its descendants arrive together and you only wait on the model. Use Persistent only if the door must always exist. Alternatively, call RequestStreamAroundAsync.

Better still, handle door touches on the server, where every part always exists.
B3:
Bugs:
1. The player is never checked. If the player left, plr is nil, plr.UserId errors inside pcall, and the code still returns PurchaseGranted. The player is charged and gets nothing.
2. The pcall result is ignored. A failed GetAsync or SetAsync still returns PurchaseGranted. The player is charged and gets nothing.
3. There is no PurchaseId idempotency. Receipts can be delivered again (for example after a timeout, or when the grant is processed but the acknowledgement is lost), so the player gets double coins.
4. GetAsync + SetAsync is a non-atomic read-modify-write. It races with other saves (the session profile, another server), so coins are lost or duplicated, and the player's normal save can overwrite it.
5. The store is keyed by a raw number (fine), but the grant isn't tied to the player's session data. Also check that only one ProcessReceipt is assigned in the game.

Correct behaviour:
- Look up the player. If there is none, return NotProcessedYet.
- In one UpdateAsync (or the session-locked profile save), check whether receipt.PurchaseId is already in the processed list. If it isn't, add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId. Both are written together.
- Return PurchaseGranted only if that save succeeded. Otherwise return NotProcessedYet.
- Never yield inside the transform.
B4:
1. Metatables don't replicate. Remote arguments are serialized: tables are deep-copied as plain data, and metatables and functions are stripped. The client receives {Name = "Rifle", Ammo = 30} with no __index, so w:Fire() is nil. (Mixed or non-string keys can also be lost.)
2. ServerStorage is never replicated to clients. An Instance argument arrives as a reference only if the client can see that instance. Muzzle lives in ServerStorage, so the client gets nil.

Fix:
- Send plain data, then rebuild the object on the client:
```lua
-- client
local w = setmetatable(data, Weapon)
-- or
local w = Weapon.new(data)
```
  Weapon is a shared ModuleScript in ReplicatedStorage.
- Put Muzzle in ReplicatedStorage (or clone it into Workspace or the character) before sending it. Or send an identifier (a name or id) and have the client look it up in ReplicatedStorage.
B5:
WorldRoot:Raycast(origin, direction) uses the length of the direction vector as the ray's range. .Unit has length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud. It almost never reaches the target.

Another common issue is the ray hitting the shooter's own character or the gun. Exclude them with RaycastParams.

Fix:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local MAX_RANGE = 300
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX_RANGE
-- or (target - origin) to stop exactly at the target
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Raycast also returns nil when nothing is hit, so keep the nil check. Validate on the server.
B6:
Cause: when the last player leaves, the server starts shutting down right away. PlayerRemoving fires, but the server can close before the yielding SetAsync finishes, so the save is cut off and lost. SetAsync is also a blind overwrite with no retry.

Standard fix: add game:BindToClose. The engine gives BindToClose callbacks about 30 seconds total.
- In BindToClose, save every remaining player in parallel (task.spawn per player) and wait for all saves, including ones already started by PlayerRemoving, with a deadline of about 25 s.
- Serialize saves per player so PlayerRemoving and BindToClose don't double-write. Track in-flight saves and wait on them.
- Use UpdateAsync with a session lock and retries with backoff, not a single SetAsync.
- Also autosave every 60-180 s, so a crash loses little.
- In Studio, skip the long wait with RunService:IsStudio().

```lua
game:BindToClose(function()
    local pending = 0
    for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
        pending += 1
        task.spawn(function()
            savePlayer(p, true)
            pending -= 1
        end)
    end
    local t = os.clock()
    while pending > 0 and os.clock() - t < 25 do
        task.wait(0.1)
    end
end)
```

```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UseAbility = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.UseAbility
local COOLDOWN = 2
local lastUse = {} -- [Player] = time

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, abilityId)
    if typeof(abilityId) ~= "string" or #abilityId > 32 then return end
```

- The cooldown is tracked on the server with os.clock, and the timestamp is set before any yielding work.
- Invalid or spammed calls are dropped without replying.
- Entries are removed in PlayerRemoving, so the table doesn't grow.

- PurchaseGranted is returned only after a successful save.

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local menu = script.Parent:WaitForChild("Menu")
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
local OPEN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)
local CLOSED = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 1.5, 0)
local isOpen = false
local current

local function open()
    isOpen = true
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    menu.Position = menu.Visible and menu.Position or CLOSED
    menu.Visible = true
    current = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = OPEN})
    current:Play()
end

local function close()
    isOpen = false
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    local t = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = CLOSED})
    current = t
    t.Completed:Connect(function(state)
        -- hide only if this tween finished and the menu is still meant to be closed
        if state == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed and not isOpen then
            menu.Visible = false
        end
    end)
    t:Play()
end
```
The Completed state check stops a reopen during the slide-out from hiding the menu. Set menu.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5) so it is centred.

B13:
- (a) Client to server buy request: a RemoteEvent, for example BuyItem:FireServer("Sword"). The request contains only intent, never the price or the balance. A RemoteFunction is fine if the UI needs a success or failure reply.
- Validation and the balance live only on the server. The server checks the item exists, reads the server-side price, checks coins in the player's server data, deducts, grants, saves and rate-limits.
- (b) Server to client update: a RemoteEvent with FireClient(player, newCoins). Simpler still, replicate the balance through leaderstats or an attribute on the Player and have the UI listen with GetPropertyChangedSignal or Changed.
- Why not server-to-client InvokeClient:
  - The server would yield until the client returns, and an exploiter can never return, which hangs the server thread forever.
  - If the client errors or leaves, the server gets an error.
  - The client controls the return value.
  - A UI update needs no reply, so a one-way FireClient or a replicated value is correct.
B14:
- Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData, read with GetJoinData / GetLocalPlayerTeleportData) passes through the client and can be spoofed. Only SourcePlaceId and the server-side join data are partly trustworthy, and even then the data was transmitted by the client. It's fine for non-authoritative hints such as the chosen map, party id, or a cosmetic loadout preference. Never use it for coins or owned items.
- DataStores are authoritative and persistent. Save the profile and release the session lock before teleporting. The match server loads the profile with the lock, so coins and owned loadout come from trusted data. They cost DataStore budget and have a small latency.
- MemoryStores are fast, short-lived (TTL) and shared across the experience. They're good for match tickets and handoff state, for example "player X chose loadout Y for match Z".

My choice:
- Keep coins and owned items in the DataStore profile, saved before teleport and loaded with a session lock at the destination.
- For the chosen loadout, either store it in the profile, or write a MemoryStore ticket with a TTL and pass only the ticket id in teleport data. The match server consumes the ticket and checks that the player owns the items.
- Use teleport data only for the ticket id and other hints.
B15:
Problems with one Script per instance (610 scripts):
- 610 script VMs and threads, with duplicated code. A bug fix means editing hundreds of copies.
- Higher memory use and startup cost, and it's hard to profile.
- Copies drift out of sync.
- Scripts inside streamed or cloned parts run unpredictably, and when a part is destroyed its connections are lost.

Tag-driven architecture (recommended):
- Tag instances with CollectionService ("Door", "Pickup", "Turret"), in Studio or when spawning.
- Write one server Script or module per behaviour, for example a DoorSystem, PickupSystem and TurretSystem. Keep shared config in attributes on each instance (for example Damage or Range).
- Each system:
  - Handles everything that exists now: for each x in GetTagged(tag), call setup(x).
  - Picks up new instances: GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag):Connect(setup). This covers runtime spawns and, on the client, instances that stream in.
  - Cleans up: GetInstanceRemovedSignal(tag):Connect(cleanup), which disconnects per-instance connections stored in a table (or a Trove/Maid), so nothing leaks.
  - Uses one Heartbeat loop over the active turrets, with throttled updates, instead of 60 separate loops.
- Server systems own the authoritative logic, such as damage, pickups and door state. Client systems handle visuals only and must expect instances to stream in and out, so they don't assume everything exists.
B16:
- Ownership: give the driver's client network ownership while they're seated: VehicleSeat occupant changes, then SetNetworkOwner(player) on the car's root assembly. That gives responsive, lag-free handling. On exit, return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)), and keep idle cars server-owned. Set it explicitly to avoid ownership flip-flop jitter.
- Risk: the owning client is authoritative over the car's physics. Exploiters can teleport, fly or speed-hack the car, skip the track, or fling other players and cars.
- What the server must still validate:
  - Speed against the car's maximum, with a margin (for example x1.35).
  - Position jumps or teleports between ticks.
  - Hovering with no ground below while not falling.
  - Lap progress through ordered server-side checkpoints, with server timestamps and minimum segment times. The server decides lap and race times and finishes.
  - Collision groups to limit flinging.
  - On repeated strikes (for example 3): revoke ownership and reset the car to the last good CFrame. Whitelist legitimate boosts and teleports.
- Never trust client-reported times or positions for rewards.
- 2026 option: Server Authority mode (AuthorityMode = Server) with client prediction. Prototype it for fast cars first.
B17:
Use an UnreliableRemoteEvent for aim and position, and lower the rate to about 10-20 Hz, interpolating on receivers.
- Each packet replaces the previous one, so losing one costs nothing.
- Also quantize and pack the data, for example angles as int16 in a buffer, and send position only when it changed.
- Better still, let the character's replicated physics carry position. Only send aim.

Constraints and how to handle them:
- Payloads over about 1,000 bytes are silently dropped. Keep each packet small and don't batch large tables.
- Packets can be lost. Never use it for state that must arrive, such as fire start and stop, ability state, or purchases. Use a reliable RemoteEvent or an attribute for those.
- Packets arrive unordered. Include a sequence number (for example 16-bit, wrap-aware) and drop stale or duplicate packets.
- The server must still validate types, finite values, unit-length directions and plausible positions, and must rate-limit per player.
- For the server's view of other players, interpolate between samples.
B18:
How:
- Split the NPCs across many Actors, for example 8-16 Actors each owning about 12-25 NPCs, because scripts inside one Actor run sequentially.
- In each Actor's script, connect with RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(fn), or call task.desynchronize(). In the parallel phase, do the read-only work: workspace:Raycast, spatial queries, path scoring and math.
- Store the results in local tables. Then call task.synchronize() and apply writes in the serial phase: setting CFrames, MoveTo, firing events, changing properties.
- Throttle: stagger NPCs over frames and don't recompute every Heartbeat when there's no need. Profile with the MicroProfiler first.

Limitations to design around:
- Most instance writes, and creating, parenting or destroying instances, are not allowed in parallel. Batch writes in the serial phase.
- Check thread-safety tags. Reads and Raycast are safe.
- require cannot run in the parallel phase. Require modules at load time.
- Shared state goes through SharedTable (string or integer keys, no Instances or functions as keys; slower than a plain table; SharedTable.update may run more than once) or Actor messages. Messages copy their arguments, so send ids rather than big snapshots.
- The order of parallel tasks is not deterministic. Parallel only pays off when compute is heavy and writes are light.
B19:
- Workspace: turn StreamingEnabled on (set in Studio; these properties can't be set from scripts).
  - StreamingMinRadius: keep the default of 64. Raise it for fast vehicles.
  - StreamingTargetRadius: keep the default of 1024, or lower it for mobile memory. It must be larger than the minimum radius.
  - StreamOutBehavior: Opportunistic (default LowMemory).
  - StreamingIntegrityMode: PauseOutsideLoadedArea (or MinimumRadiusPause).
  - ModelStreamingBehavior: Improved.
  - Per-model ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models whose parts must arrive together, Persistent only for the few things that must always exist (sparingly), PersistentPerPlayer through AddPersistentPlayer, and Nonatomic by default.
- Scripts that assumed everything was loaded:
  - Replace direct dot-indexing into Workspace with WaitForChild plus a timeout, on Atomic models rather than every descendant.
  - Better: CollectionService tags with GetTagged, GetInstanceAddedSignal and GetInstanceRemovedSignal, so they handle stream-in and stream-out.
  - Keep client state on the Player or in ReplicatedStorage, not on workspace parts.
  - Before server teleports or cutscenes, use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync.
  - Server scripts still see everything. Move authoritative logic there.
  - Clean up connections when instances stream out.
- Never turn streaming off again to fix bugs.
B20:
Cause:
- 80 players x 1 write every 5 s is about 960 writes per minute, all landing on the same ticks.
- Over budget, requests queue. Each queue holds about 30 requests, and a full queue fails new ones immediately with errors 301-306 (302 = queue full), so saves are lost.
- The per-experience write budget is 300 + 20 x CCU per minute. The per-server default is 60 + 40 x players, and a burst on one tick exceeds it.
- Per-key limits also apply: writes are capped at 4 MB per minute per key and each request rounds up to the next KB. Writing a key every 5 s is wasteful anyway.
- SetAsync with no lock also risks overwriting data.

Better design:
- Keep data in memory in a session-locked profile and mark it dirty when it changes.
- Autosave every 60-180 s, staggered per player with a random offset or jitter, and only if dirty.
- Also save on leave (PlayerRemoving), on shutdown (BindToClose, in parallel), and right after important events such as purchases or trades, debounced to at least 2 s apart.
- Use UpdateAsync with retries and exponential backoff, never instant retries.
- Check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before bulk saves.
- Keep profiles small.

B22:
- Three core instances:
  - InputContext: a group of actions with Enabled, Priority and Sink.
  - InputAction: Type can be Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, Direction3D or ViewportPosition.
  - InputBinding: a child of the action that maps an input to it, through KeyCode (keyboard or gamepad), UIButton (a GuiButton for touch), modifiers and Scale.
- How an action signals a press:
  - For Bool actions, InputAction.Pressed and InputAction.Released fire.
  - StateChanged fires for every action type.
  - InputAction:GetState() polls the current value (true while held, or a vector).
- Menu precedence:
  - Create a menu InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay and default player-script contexts, and set Sink = true. Its bound keys are then consumed and lower-priority contexts don't receive them.
  - Enable the menu context while the menu is open and disable it on close.
  - To block movement entirely, disable the gameplay context. Don't use PlayerModule GetControls().
  - Default player scripts move onto IAS through Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem.
B23:
It is the engine's UI Styling system, which works like CSS for GuiObjects.
- Instances:
  - StyleSheet: a container of rules.
  - StyleRule: has a Selector string and properties set with StyleRule:SetProperties({...}). Rules can be nested.
  - StyleLink: links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui or other UI tree so its rules apply. Only one sheet applies per tree.
  - StyleDerive: lets one StyleSheet inherit another, for example a theme that derives from base tokens.
  - StyleQuery: conditional rules, for example by screen size or preferred input.
- How styles reach the UI: a StyleLink connects a sheet to the UI tree. Each rule's selector matches GuiObjects in that tree, and the engine applies the properties. Selectors can match:
  - The class name, for example "TextButton".
  - A CollectionService tag, for example ".PrimaryButton".
  - The instance name, for example "#Title".
  - GuiState pseudo-classes such as ":Hover".
  - Child modifiers such as "::UICorner" to add corners or strokes.
- Tokens: define attributes on a tokens StyleSheet, for example tokens:SetAttribute("Primary", Color3.fromRGB(...)), and reference them in rules as "$Primary", for example BackgroundColor3 = "$Primary". Swapping or deriving a sheet with the same token names re-themes everything, such as light and dark modes.
- Don't also set the same properties from code. The Studio Style Editor was still in beta as of late 2026.
B24:
- Method: an age check, usually facial age estimation (a selfie video in the Roblox app, processed by a vendor). A government ID check, or for younger users parental controls, can correct the estimate. Chat is live with this check worldwide since January 2026, after it started in late 2025. Users who don't check can't use chat.
- Age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20, and 21+.
- Restrictions:
  - By default, users can chat only with their own age group and the groups directly next to it (one above and one below).
  - Under-16s are kept apart from adults.
  - Trusted Connections, for users 13 and up who know each other, can widen this.
  - Under-9s have chat off by default unless a parent enables it.
- Developers get no API that exposes age, so don't build gameplay that depends on chat.
